facts.text: In the breeding season the cattle egret develops orange-buff plumes and its bill, legs and irises turn bright red for a short time before pairing.
facts.quote: During the breeding season, adults of the nominate western subspecies develop orange-buff plumes on the back, breast and crown, and the bill, legs and irises become bright red for a brief period prior to pairing.

facts.text: The cattle egret usually gives only a quiet, throaty rick-rack call at the breeding colony and is otherwise largely silent.
facts.quote: This species gives a quiet, throaty rick-rack call at the breeding colony, but is otherwise largely silent.

facts.text: When foraging beside cattle, the egret is 3.6 times more successful at catching prey than when feeding alone.
facts.quote: When foraging with cattle, it has been shown to be 3.6 times more successful in capturing prey than when foraging alone.

facts.text: The cattle egret removes ticks and flies from cattle, benefiting both the bird and the beast.
facts.quote: The cattle egret removes ticks and flies from cattle and consumes them. This benefits both species

facts.text: On some islands, cattle egrets prey on the eggs and chicks of terns and other seabirds.
facts.quote: On islands with seabird colonies, it will prey on the eggs and chicks of terns and other seabirds.

facts.text: The male displays in a tree by shaking a twig and sky-pointing with his bill raised vertically, and the pair forms over three or four days.
facts.quote: The male displays in a tree in the colony, using a range of ritualised behaviour such as shaking a twig and sky-pointing (raising his bill vertically upwards), and the pair forms over three or four days.

facts.text: The nest is an untidy stick platform built by both parents, with the male collecting sticks and the female arranging them, and stick-stealing is rife.
facts.quote: The nest is a small untidy platform of sticks in a tree or shrub constructed by both parents. Sticks are collected by the male and arranged by the female, and stick-stealing is rife.

facts.text: In Australia, cattle egrets reduce the number of flies bothering cattle by pecking them straight off the skin.
facts.quote: A study in Australia found that cattle egrets reduced the number of flies that bothered cattle by pecking them directly off the skin.
